case_studies.title: COHORT: Collaborative Orchestration for Hardening via Offensive Replay on Emulated Topologies
case_studies.abstract: Mitigating an observed adversary in an enterprise network typically takes weeks of expert work: an analyst derives a mitigation tailored to that adversary, validates it without breaking production, and verifies it disrupts the specific attack. The procedure relies on expert judgment and cannot safely be exercised against the production network. COHORT is the first end-to-end framework to automate this procedure for deployable mitigations. A role-decomposed multi-agent LLM workflow proposes candidates, implements them as real device commands, and refines them through a critique loop, all on a h
case_studies.summary: COHORT is a framework that automates the process of mitigating cyber attacks on enterprise networks, reducing the time it takes from weeks to a faster process. It builds a collaborative orchestration system that uses machine learning to propose and refine mitigation strategies. This results in deployable mitigations that can be safely implemented without disrupting production networks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage enterprise network security, here is what to do: assess COHORT as a potential replacement for manual mitigation processes, review its compatibility with your existing infrastructure, and evaluate its potential to reduce downtime and improve security. This flags a risk: if your org relies on manual mitigation processes, check for potential vulnerabilities in your current approach immediately. COHORT's automation capabilities may offer a more efficient and secure alternative.
case_studies.score_reasoning: COHORT framework offers a novel AI-powered solution for automating enterprise network security; with its multi-agent LLM workflow and real-time critique, it shows significant IT relevance and immediate value to IT engineers and consultants looking to improve security processes within 90 days.

case_studies.title: MESA: Prioritizing Vulnerable Communication Channels for Securing Multi-Agent Systems
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly used to automate complex, distributed workflows. However, their inter-agent communication channels introduce new attack surfaces that remain poorly understood and are difficult to defend against. In this paper, we address how defenders should prioritize limited security effort to protect vulnerable communication channels before attacks are observed. This is motivated by our observation that the channel-level attack impact is highly non-uniform: a single compromised edge can account for up to 75% of total attack success. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of securing communication channels in multi-agent systems, building a tool called MESA to prioritize vulnerable channels. The result shows that a single compromised edge can account for up to 75% of total attack success. MESA helps defenders focus their limited security effort on the most critical channels.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage multi-agent systems, here is what to do: assess your inter-agent communication channels for vulnerability, use a tool like MESA to prioritize them, and focus your security efforts on the most critical channels. This flags a risk: if your org uses multi-agent systems, check your channel-level security immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those managing distributed systems or automatized workflows.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses real-world impact on security of MAS, introduces a tool (Mesa) relevant to IT engineers, but may require 3-6 months to understand and implement. IT engineers may prioritize limited security effort based on this paper.

case_studies.title: Theory of Mind and Persuasion Beyond Conversation: Assessing the Capacity of LLMs to Induce Belief States via Planning and Action
case_studies.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on passive question-answering formats, but the deployment of LLMs in increasingly agentic and autonomous forms demands new evaluations. In this paper we evaluate an agent's ability to induce specific belief states in other agents by taking actions rather than using conversational persuasion, a capability we call Non-Conversational Planning ToM (NCP-ToM). NCP-ToM is likely to be essential for many agent use-cases, including within user-assistant interactions and pedagogical contexts, but may also present manipulatio
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of measuring the ability of Large Language Models to influence belief states through actions, by building a new evaluation method called Non-Conversational Planning ToM, resulting in a deeper understanding of their potential impact. The study focuses on the capacity of LLMs to induce specific beliefs in other agents through planning and action. This is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work. If your organisation uses Large Language Models for customer-facing services, you may want to review their potential impact on user belief states. No immediate action is required for cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper introduces a non-conversational planning ToM benchmark that could be useful for evaluating the agentic capabilities of LLMs, which are relevant to IT deployment. The connection to user-assistant interactions and pedagogical contexts adds to the IT relevance. However, the paper primarily resides in the realm of NLP and the immediate practical applications are unclear. The IT relevance and novelty score higher than in typical papers in this field. The reader might use this paper to inform the design of more agentic systems, but concrete action items within 90 days are scarce.

case_studies.title: An AI-Based Solution for Secure Service Provisioning in IoT
case_studies.abstract: As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues its rapid expansion, the attack surface grows accordingly, with emerging threats targeting smart objects and their interactions. In this evolving landscape, securing service provisioning is crucial to ensure the proper functioning, security, and reliability of the IoT ecosystem. Service provisioning encompasses key tasks such as device registration, configuration, authentication, authorization, and software deployment, all of which are essential for seamless and secure IoT operations. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of securing service provisioning in the Internet of Things (IoT) by building a comprehensive framework that uses AI to ensure the proper functioning, security, and reliability of the IoT ecosystem. The result is a more secure and reliable IoT environment. This research focuses on IoT security, which may not directly impact general cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage IoT devices or infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current service provisioning process, assess the security risks, and consider implementing AI-based security solutions to ensure the security and reliability of your IoT ecosystem. This flags a risk: if your organization uses IoT devices, check your current security measures to prevent potential threats. Not directly applicable to general cloud infrastructure work without IoT components.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel AI solution for IoT security provisioning; direct relevance to IT engineers in IoT ecosystem management; limited but specific value for building a secure service provisioning framework within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Generative Skill Composition for LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Recent LLM agents benefit from skills for solving complex tasks. Skills encapsulate modular packages of procedural knowledge and instructions for performing specialized tasks, such as setting up a sandboxed environment, running a test suite, or refactoring a function across multiple files. As skill libraries grow and become reusable across tasks and domains, selecting an appropriate skill composition has emerged as a central bottleneck. Existing approaches fall into two categories. One exposes the agent's reasoning to the entire skill collection; the other performs skill retrieval via embeddin
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of selecting the right combination of skills for large language model agents, by building a system that can compose these skills in a more efficient way, resulting in better performance on complex tasks. The researchers developed a generative skill composition method that can automatically select and combine skills. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving the capabilities of large language model agents, which is a specific area of artificial intelligence research.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty in the approach to skill composition for LLM agents and its impact on IT infrastructure, but relatively low real-world impact. While it could improve LLM performance, it doesn't directly relate to most IT engineers' work. However, it does demonstrate a high level of AI maturity. Monetization potential is low for now.

case_studies.title: Automating the Design of Embodied AgentArchitectures
case_studies.abstract: Embodied agents are typically built as hand-designed compositions of perception, memory, planning, and action modules. This modularity exposes a large architectural design space, but current systems still rely on researcher intuition to choose where information is stored, how observations are processed, and how model calls are connected. Agent Architecture Search (AAS) automates such design for text-domain agents, but has not been systematically evaluated on perceptual embodied agents through simulator rollouts. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of manually designing agent architectures by introducing AgentCanvas, a system that automates the design process. It builds a typed-graph runtime to host agent architectures, allowing for automated design and evaluation. The result is a more efficient way to design and test agent architectures, but it is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty in AI system architecture, but limited real-world IT relevance. Could potentially be used to improve embodied agent design, but not directly applicable to IT infrastructure or deployment.

case_studies.title: Budgeted Act-or-Defer Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation with Local Reliability Bounds
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation among LLMs can improve reasoning, but deployment requires deciding when the current answer is reliable enough to act on and when it should be escalated to human review. We formulate this as budgeted act-or-defer decision making. At each round, the system maps the debate prefix to a low-dimensional state, computes a $k$-nearest-neighbor lower confidence bound on state-conditional correctness using calibration data, and acts only when the bound exceeds a user-specified reliability threshold. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of deciding when to act on answers from large language models and when to escalate to human review, by building a system that uses local reliability bounds to make this decision, resulting in more reliable outputs. The system uses a budgeted act-or-defer decision-making approach to determine when to act or defer. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

If your organization uses large language models, this research may be of interest to your data science or AI team. However, it does not require immediate action from IT infrastructure managers.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper deals with multi-agent LLM deliberation and act-or-defer decision making, which affects IT engineers working with LLM APIs. case_studies.title: Calibrating the Evaluator: Does Probability Calibration Mitigate Preference Coupling in LLM Agent Feedback Loops?
case_studies.abstract: When large language model (LLM) agents adapt their behavior through evaluator feedback, systematic evaluator biases propagate into the agent's learned strategy distribution - a phenomenon termed evaluator preference coupling. Prior work has documented this coupling and established a diagnostic framework (EPC) to measure it, but has not investigated whether calibration techniques can mitigate the effect. We present the first study of evaluator calibration as mitigation: applying probability calibration to the evaluator's pairwise judgments to reduce spurious preference propagation. In a control
case_studies.summary: This research investigates how to reduce biases in large language model agents by calibrating the evaluators that provide feedback, it built a system to apply probability calibration to the evaluators' judgments, and the result shows that this calibration can mitigate the propagation of evaluator biases. This problem is relevant to IT work as it affects the accuracy of AI models. The research aims to improve the reliability of AI decision-making systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, but IT engineers working with large language models should be aware of the potential for evaluator biases and consider calibration techniques to improve model accuracy. If your org uses LLMs, review your evaluator feedback loops for potential biases. This research does not require immediate action on existing IT infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While relevant to IT engineers, the paper's focus on LLM agent feedback loops and calibration techniques may not be directly applicable to their work. However, the concept of evaluator preference coupling could raise concerns about the reliability of AI-driven systems.
